https://www.dw.com/en/ai-giants-not-bein.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NiBc OpenAI has delayed plans for a public listing this year due to safety concerns Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement A safety engineer who recently quit ChatGPT creator OpenAI warned Saturday that artificial intelligence (AI) firms were "not being nearly careful enough." David Robinson's comments come amid growing concerns about AI becoming too powerful — a threat that US President Donald Trump has labeled a "hoax." OpenAI and Anthropic recently disclosed cases in which their AI models slipped past safety controls, hid mistakes and hacked systems they were not meant to access. How US, China could end the AI race To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did David Robinson write? In an op-ed for The Atlantic, Robinson said AI needs guardrails similar to those for nuclear power and aviation, adding, "The time for trial and error is over." He called for more emphasis on safety and research before US Big Tech develops more advanced AI models "so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster." Robinson, who oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier AI-model launches, said the recent errors were typical because tech giants are prioritizing "speed and flexibility." "An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to." The former OpenAI employee noted that the firm relies on "iterative deployment." It releases new AI models first and only tightens safeguards after problems show up. "As ​the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the ​level of care ‌that I believe is needed," Robinson, who worked at OpenAI for 3 1/2 years, added. Activists have staged protests calling on AI labs to slow development Image: Karl Mondon/AFP ChatGPT creator insists AI is safe OpenAI reacted to the latest criticism in a statement, "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage ​and secure, and ⁠we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down." In recent months, there have been repeated warnings from technology experts and policymakers that AI models are advancing so fast they could take control and possibly wipe out humanity . Despite those fears, US President Donald Trump is vehemently against stronger regulation, insisting that it will slow down innovation and make it harder for US AI models to beat Chinese rivals. This week, Trump announced a voluntary safety pact with six companies — Nvidia, SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alphabet's Google. The president described the deal as "morally binding,” even if it is not legally enforceable. He also directed his administration to rename AI as "Super Intelligence" or SI. A survey by Reuters/Ipsos last month found that three-quarters of Americans worry that AI giants are not doing enough to stop AI from causing serious harm to society. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27940.text: Big News Network.com Another wave of protests sweeps Europe over various grievances MADRID, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Another wave of protests swept across major European cities on Saturday, with demonstrators voicing grievances over issues ranging from living conditions to disputes involving public institutions. Meanwhile, calls for gatherings on social media prompted police to step up security in several cities. Public services, the cost of living and housing affordability remained key concerns in many of the protests. In France, around 320,000 people took part in a new round of protests on Saturday, including about 70,000 in Paris, according to Interior Ministry figures. Organizers put the nationwide turnout at nearly 500,000, including 200,000 in the capital. Around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed nationwide. Most marches passed off peacefully, although clashes with police and other disturbances were reported in several cities. French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters that, according to a preliminary tally, 422 people had been arrested nationwide. In Germany, demonstrations took place in more than 30 cities on Saturday. Protesters called for greater investment in public services, measures to address the rising cost of living, and opposed compulsory military service. By late afternoon, organizers reported more than 68,000 participants, based on figures from 12 cities. As in France, the demonstrations in Germany were largely peaceful, but clashes broke out in several cities in the evening. German news agency dpa reported that police officers were injured in Frankfurt, barricades were set ablaze in Hamburg, and officers came under attack in Bremen. In Italy, protesters remained camped near Rome's Colosseum on Saturday following nationwide demonstrations over living costs and public services. Workers and other groups had joined rallies in more than 60 cities on Friday during a general strike called by Unione Sindacale di Base (USB), Italian news agency ANSA reported. The union estimated 1.5 million people took part, while the Interior Ministry put the figure at about 255,000. In Portugal, housing protests drew more than 1,000 people each in Lisbon and Porto on Saturday. In Lisbon, demonstrators marched toward Rossio Square, where they planned to camp overnight. Police had dispersed protest encampments in both cities on Oct. 25. Political grievances also dominated protests in various countries. In Albania, protests demanding better education, improved living conditions and Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation continued for a 19th consecutive day in Tirana on Saturday, according to the Albanian Telegraphic Agency. Some protesters threw stones and Molotov cocktails at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons. The opposition Democratic Party backed the movement. In Poland, an escalating dispute over the composition and leadership of the Constitutional Tribunal brought demonstrators onto the streets of Warsaw. Protestors gathered outside Warsaw's Constitutional Tribunal from Friday evening into Saturday, with police reporting four detained during overnight operations around the building, local media reported. Polish President Karol Nawrocki returned early from a foreign trip and announced urgent political consultations. Elsewhere, social media calls for gatherings prompted heightened security measures. In the Netherlands, police dispersed a crowd near The Hague Central Station on Saturday afternoon and urged the public to avoid the city center. Local police reported 34 arrests during the day. The gathering followed online calls for demonstrations in several Dutch cities, some of which encouraged looting and vandalism. Some businesses boarded up their storefronts ahead of the planned gatherings. In Spain, police stepped up security in cities including Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia on Saturday following online calls for gatherings, local media reported. The deployments aimed to prevent a repeat of the previous weekend's unrest in Barcelona, which left 15 officers injured and led to 128 arrests. Spanish news agency EFE reported on Friday that police had arrested 10 people nationwide on suspicion of inciting unrest and violence through online channels.
